children: Five months, three attempts and one city on the map. The dates below come from repositories, logs and data releases.
The first Industrial Atlas starts life as a browser map of workshops and industrial land across the United Kingdom, built on OpenStreetMap.
Work turns to Hamilton and the Niagara Peninsula. Every candidate source is checked against its live endpoint and written down with counts, fields and licences.
A reconnaissance of the twelve Niagara municipalities finds one shared catalogue of 534 datasets instead of twelve portals.
Hamilton's open data catalogue is swept: 463 datasets.
A short spike tests the approach on Waterloo Region and Rochester, New York.
The first Hamilton–Niagara atlas is paused at a clean boundary, with a unit index of 445,075 parcels, buildings and addresses built and nothing yet drawn.
HeavyMap begins as its own project.
The vocabulary for describing what we know about a parcel is written down as rules a machine can check. Counts for Brantford, Brant County and Norfolk County are verified by hand.
A coverage study lists 606 dataset rows that touch Hamilton.

The big day: the Hamilton catalogue is written, about a million features are pulled, every parcel gets a stable identifier, eleven overlay layers are joined to every parcel, and the first local map tiles are built.
A beta gate for Hamilton is agreed: the checks a city must pass before it opens.
The first static map of Hamilton's lower city and harbourfront.
A self-hosted basemap in light and dark, and the first versioned Hamilton data release.
Building permits go on the map, freight and infrastructure sources are profiled, and building footprints are ranked within their parcels.
The public data discovery method is written down, and this Journey begins.
